pages.text:
*Garden Log, Day 365: Growing: everything. Waiting: still. (Better.)*

A week later, the rain had stopped, but the air still felt heavy and wet, pressing down on the concrete like a damp towel. Ms. Vandermeer stood at the gap in the fence, her yellow raincoat looking too bright for the grey evening. She had no charts and no clipboard, only her hands clasped in front of her while she watched the moss on the wall.

I was there with the watering can, coming out of habit because the sky was clearing and the soil looked thirsty.

"Ms. Vandermeer," I said.

She turned, and her hair was plastered to her face in thin, dark strips, making her look smaller than she does in the council chambers.

"I saw you leave," she said, her voice quiet and stripped of its usual brisk efficiency. "I wanted to see what you were protecting."

I shifted the heavy can in my hands. "The rules are simple. One true thing, said aloud. And then you sit down."

She looked at me, then at the bench under the pear tree. "I have planned for twenty years," she said. "I have never once gone to look at what I planned."

She walked in without asking permission and sat on the bench, where the wood hummed with a low, warm vibration that I could feel in the soles of my boots. She put her hands on her knees and stayed there, breathing, while the rain started again, soft and steady.
pages.image: A woman in a bright yellow raincoat sits on a wooden bench under a large pear tree in a green garden, hands resting on her knees, looking contemplative and quiet; rain falls softly around her.

pages.text:
Spring did not arrive with a bang, but it crept in, one green shoot at a time, like a student who arrives late and hopes nobody noticed the delay. The concrete of Lowell Court seemed to soften as the grass in the car park turned a vivid, impossible green, while the single fenced tree bloomed with white flowers that hung low and smelled of honey and old paper.

We had one hundred and fifty volunteers for the first day. Mrs. Ilves was there, her knitting done, holding a scarf nine meters long, a thick tangle of red and green wool that she draped over Mr. Osei’s shoulders with the firmness of a general presenting a medal.

"For the cold," she said, her voice sharp with pride.

Mr. Osei, who had not entered his own garden in thirty years, stood in the Spring Room holding a trowel. He looked like a man trying to remember how to hold a tool without breaking it, his hands hovering just above the soil as if they might be electric.

Ms. Vandermeer signed the trial agreement. It was a simple document: one year, a community allotment, no parking, just dirt. She signed it with a pen that clicked twice when she was done, a small, satisfying sound in the quiet air.
pages.image: Mr. Osei, the very tall older man with a grey moustache and blue overalls, wears a very long knitted red and green scarf while standing in the garden holding a small trowel, with a crowd of people planting in the background

pages.text:
The Winter Room was under glass, and the light came in sideways, golden and dusty. I knelt by the third row of clay pots. My knees ached, but I did not care.

I had forgotten the true thing I had said when I planted it. I remembered the seed, a small, hard thing, but the words were gone. I had said them to the soil, and the soil had kept them.

I waited.

A tiny shape broke the surface of the dirt. It was brown-green, wet, and incredibly small. It looked fragile, like a hair. Then it straightened. It was about the height of my thumbnail.

I pulled out my tape measure. My hands were shaking, just a little. I held the metal tape against the shoot. Two centimeters.

It was nothing. It was everything. It was the most enormous thing I had ever seen.
pages.image: A close-up of a hand holding a small metal tape measure against a tiny green sprout emerging from dark soil in a clay pot, the background blurred with soft golden light from a window.

pages.text:
They were standing in a half-circle around me. Yusuf, Theo, Nadia, and Mr. Osei. They were silent. Even Yusuf, who usually made a noise like a static-filled radio, was still.

Gherkin was at my elbow, moving with the slowness of a glacier, his mossy shell catching the light. He opened his mouth, then closed it, then opened it again. It took a full minute.

"Mm," he said.

I waited.

"There," he finished.

It was the shortest thing he had ever said to me, but it was also the most important. He had not said "Mm. Not yet." He had said "There," as if he were pointing at the only fact that mattered.

I looked up at him. "It took a year," I said.

He blinked, slowly. "Mm. Yes," he said. "And?"
pages.image: A large tortoise with a mossy shell looks up at a kneeling girl, while a group of children and an adult stand in a semi-circle behind them, all focused on the tortoise with expressions of quiet awe.

pages.text:
That night, the window stood open, letting in the raw smell of wet earth from beyond the concrete. It mingled with the yeast-heavy scent of Baba’s warm bread, which was cooling on the table. I sat on the floor with my notebook in my lap and read the first entry again. *Growing: nothing. Waiting: everything.*

I laughed, a small, dry sound that felt like shaking out a bag of stale chips. The paper was crisp under my thumb as I flipped the page.

*Day 366. Planted: one seed. True thing: I can wait.*

I closed the notebook, stood up, and walked to the door. I took the stairs down ninety-two steps, counting each one in the dark until my feet hit the cold concrete of the ground floor.

I went out to the garden. I poured the water. It was enough.
